title: The LLD Interview and How to Approach It
subtitle: From one sentence to classes, a diagram and running code

scenes.title: The LLD Interview and How to Approach It
scenes.subtitle: From one sentence to classes, a diagram and running code

steps.say: Welcome to episode one of the LLD Workshop. LLD means low-level design. By the end you'll know what this round is, how it's scored, and a repeatable method that turns one vague sentence into a class diagram and working Java.
First a complete tiny answer, a music playlist. Then the method, with every step applied to one running example: a parking lot, the most asked question in this round.
Keep the chapter one notes open beside the video. When I say pause and think, really pause.

scenes.title: What the LLD round is

steps.say: Concept one. Imagine an interviewer says: design a parking lot. Then they stop talking. What are they actually asking you for?

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.1 What this round is, and what this handbook covers

scenes.title: Designing the classes inside one program
bullets: One app, 45 to 60 minutes, someone watching
Class, object: a type and one instance of it
Responsibility: one job, one sentence
Relationship: uses, holds, owns, extends; UML draws it
System design = city plan; LLD = floor plan

steps.say: The low-level design round gives you one application to design while someone watches, usually in forty-five to sixty minutes. A parking lot, a vending machine, a chess game.
You design the classes inside the program. A class is a named type holding data, called fields, and methods that work on it. An object is one instance with real values.
A responsibility is the one job a class does, in a single sentence. A relationship is how two classes connect: one uses, holds, owns or extends the other.
U-M-L, the Unified Modeling Language, is the standard set of symbols for drawing classes. A design pattern is a named, reusable answer to a recurring problem.
Analogy: system design is the city plan, roads and power. Low-level design is the floor plan of one house: which rooms, and which doors connect them.

scenes.title: Same parking lot, two different rounds

steps.say: Same product, two zoom levels. Low-level design stays inside one application. System design spans many machines.
The vocabulary: classes, interfaces and patterns here, versus load balancers, databases, caches and queues there.
The output: a class diagram plus code, versus an architecture diagram plus capacity numbers.
The question: design the classes for a parking lot, versus a parking service for ten million users. Practising one gives little for the other.

scenes.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Bound the problem: requirements + out of scope
Pick classes with exactly one job each
Code the core flows until they run
Name the pattern used and the one rejected

steps.say: After this handbook you'll do four things. Turn design a parking lot into a bounded requirement list with an out-of-scope list.
Pick classes with exactly one job each, and connect them correctly.
Code the Java behind the core flows until it runs.
And name the pattern you used, the one you rejected, and why. The reusable part is the method, not memorised answers.

scenes.title: Who this is for, and what you need
bullets: For: anyone facing LLD, OOD or machine coding
Need: one OO language, all examples Java 21
Not needed: UML, system design
Basics: list, map, set, queue, heap

steps.say: Concept two. This is for anyone facing this round, especially if you write object-oriented code daily but have never defended a class diagram out loud.
You need one object-oriented language, enough that a class with a constructor, the method that sets up a new object, reads easily. Examples are Java twenty-one.
You don't need U-M-L or system design. This round stays inside one running program.

Basic data structures are enough. A list keeps order, a map looks up by key, a set has no duplicates, a queue is first in first out, a heap gives the smallest item fast. Maps and lists will be your in-memory storage.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.1 Who this is for, and what you need

scenes.title: How the interview runs

steps.say: Concept three. The interviewer says one sentence and goes quiet. Nothing tells you how many classes, whether to code, or how long you have. That silence is the hard part, so let's learn the shape of the round.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.2 How the interview runs

steps.say: Two flavours. The object-oriented design round, O-O-D, runs forty-five to sixty minutes. Machine coding is about ninety minutes of coding, two hours with review.
O-O-D happens on a whiteboard or shared doc. Machine coding happens in your own I-D-E, your code editor.
O-O-D produces requirements, a class diagram and code for two or three flows. Machine coding produces a complete running program.
Machine coding stores data in memory, in maps and lists, unless asked otherwise.
O-O-D is a continuous conversation. Machine coding is mostly silent coding, then a demo.
O-O-D judges scope, responsibilities and trade-offs. Machine coding judges working code, data models, interfaces and extensibility.
The typical failures: talking without converging, versus not finishing or one giant class.

scenes.title: Machine-coding vocabulary
bullets: Data models: Ticket, Spot
Service interface: park, exit
Extensibility: new vehicle = new value, no rewrite
Edge cases: full, empty, negative, duplicate
Thread safety: two gates at once stay correct

steps.say: Machine-coding words, with our parking lot. Data models hold the problem's data: Ticket, Spot.
The service interface is the public methods a caller uses: park and exit.
Extensibility: an electric vehicle type is a new value, not edits everywhere.
Edge cases: an empty lot, a full lot, a negative time, a duplicate ticket.
Thread safety: staying correct when two entry gates, two threads, run at once. A thread is an independent line of execution.

scenes.title: The five core steps
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["1. Clarify requirements"] --> B["2. Actors and use cases"]
  B --> C["3. Find the classes"]
  C --> D["4. Connect the classes"]
  D --> E["5. Write the code"]
scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.2 How it works: the five core steps

steps.say: Concept four, the heart of the method. Every answer follows five core steps, in this order. Clarify the requirements. Find the actors and use cases. Find the classes. Connect the classes. Write the code.
Order matters more than speed. Skip step one, and in step three you'll invent classes no requirement asked for. Let's walk each step on the parking lot so you see it happen.

scenes.title: The five steps, applied to a parking lot

head: Step
Parking lot
rows: Floors, spot types, pay, refuse if full
Customer parks, pays. Admin adds floor
Lot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, Rate
Lot owns floors, floor owns spots

steps.say: Step one, clarify. For the parking lot: multiple floors, five spot types, pay at exit, refuse when full, about ten lines.
Step two, actors and use cases. An actor is anyone outside who uses it, a use case is one thing they do. Customer takes a ticket. Admin adds a floor.
Step three, classes, one job each: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, Rate.
Step four, connect them. A lot owns floors, a floor owns spots, a ticket points at one spot.
Step five, code the two or three main flows: park, exit and pricing. Not every class at full depth.

scenes.title: Time-boxing a 45-minute round

steps.say: Concept five, time-boxing. Clarify requirements: five to eight minutes, ending with eight to twelve lines plus out of scope.
Actors and use cases: three to five minutes.
Find the classes: eight to ten minutes.
Connect them: eight to ten minutes, with multiplicity, meaning how many of each.
Code: twelve to fifteen minutes for two or three methods. Up to a quarter of the hour passes before you name a class. Nobody finishes the whole product. You're judged on the part you built properly.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.2 Time-boxing

steps.say: Machine coding: five to ten minutes reading, then requirements as a comment at the top of Main dot java.
Ten to fifteen minutes modelling entities, enums and interfaces that compile. An enum is a type with a fixed list of values, like compact and large.
Thirty to forty minutes on one happy path end to end, meaning the main flow with valid input. Park a car, exit, print the fee.
Fifteen to twenty on remaining features and edge cases.
Five to ten on polish and a demo script.
And five minutes buffer, never zero. Get something running by halfway.

scenes.title: What the interviewer is actually judging
bullets: Did you bound the problem?
One job per class, one sentence
Right relationships: hold, own, extend
Code matches the diagram
An explained trade-off

steps.say: Concept six, what's scored. One: did you bound the problem? Saying reservations are out beats a sprawling design.
Two: one job per class, in one sentence. If not, it's two classes glued together.
Three: right relationships. A lot owns its floors, a ticket only points at a spot.
Four: does the code match the diagram?
Five: can you explain a trade-off? Machine coding adds: it runs, it's modular, it handles bad input. Perfect U-M-L isn't graded. The model is graded.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.2 What the interviewer is actually judging

scenes.title: Sizing a parking lot answer
scenes.caption: Depth on two or three flows beats breadth on twelve classes

steps.say: A parking lot has about twelve requirements, twelve classes and fifteen relationships.
Only three carry the main flows: issue a ticket, hold a vehicle, price the stay. Write those properly, name the rest in a sentence. Writing all twelve at equal depth is the costliest mistake.

scenes.title: A complete answer in five minutes

steps.say: Concept seven. Before any more theory, let's see a complete answer. The question: design a music playlist. It's small on purpose, but the bigger case studies later follow the identical outline.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.3 A complete answer in five minutes

scenes.title: Playlist step 1: requirements
bullets: Songs in a playlist; order matters
Ask for the next song; track position
Shuffle changes the play order
Out of scope: accounts, downloads, storage, audio

steps.say: Step one. Three clarifying questions give three requirements. Songs sit in a playlist, and order matters.
You can ask for the next song, so the player tracks a position.
Shuffle changes the play order.
Out of scope, said out loud: accounts, downloads, storage, the audio. That list earns credit too.

scenes.title: Playlist steps 2 and 3: actors and classes
bullets: Actor: the listener
Song: data. Playlist: songs in order
PlayOrder: interface, picks the next position
InOrder and Shuffled: two ordering rules
Player: holds playlist, order, position

steps.say: Step two, the only actor is the listener: add a song, play next, switch shuffle on. Actors reveal which classes must exist.
Step three, classes. Song holds title, artist and length. Playlist holds songs in order, it doesn't play them.
PlayOrder is an interface, a set of methods with no implementation. Its job: pick the next position.
InOrder walks positions in order. Shuffled uses an order decided once, up front.
Player holds a playlist, an order and the current position. Key insight: a rule that can vary becomes its own type, and Player never knows which version it holds.

scenes.title: Playlist step 4: connect them
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P["Player"] -->|"plays"| L["Playlist"]
  L -->|"owns many"| S["Song"]
  P -->|"uses"| O["PlayOrder interface"]
  I["InOrder"] -.->|"implements"| O
  H["Shuffled"] -.->|"implements"| O
scenes.caption: Player depends on the interface, never on InOrder or Shuffled

steps.say: Step four, connect them. Three facts an interviewer checks. The arrow from Playlist to Song says owns many: the playlist owns its songs, and they go when it goes. That's called composition. In the book's U-M-L diagram it's drawn as a filled diamond, with a star meaning many.
The arrow from Player to PlayOrder says uses: the player relies on an ordering without owning it. And notice it touches only the interface, never InOrder or Shuffled.
The dashed arrows say InOrder and Shuffled implement PlayOrder. In U-M-L that's a dashed line with a hollow triangle. Add a third rule later, and it's one extra box. Nothing already drawn changes.

scenes.title: Playlist step 5: the code, in words
bullets: PlayOrder: first and after, NONE at the end
InOrder: current plus one
Shuffled: order injected, so it's testable
Player: never asks which order it holds
Song is a record; Playlist keeps its list private

steps.say: Step five, the code, explained in words. PlayOrder has two methods: first, which gives the first position to play, and after, which gives the position after the current one. Both return a constant called NONE, meaning minus one, when there's nothing left.
InOrder's first returns zero unless the list is empty. Its after returns current plus one, or NONE at the end.

Shuffled is given its order as a list, say positions two, zero, one, instead of calling a random generator. So the output is identical every run, which makes it testable. In production you'd inject a random generator with a fixed seed. Inject means hand it in from outside, usually through the constructor.

Player's playNext asks the order for first on the first call, and for after on later calls. At the end, it stays at the end. Notice: nothing in Player tests which mode is active. Its only if statements track where it is.

Song is a Java record: an immutable data carrier whose constructor and accessors are generated, and its constructor rejects a blank title or a non-positive length. Playlist keeps its list private. That's encapsulation: data reachable only through the class's own methods.
Here's the real run. Three songs: Sunrise by Ada Lane, Blue Line by The Meridians, Paper Boats by Nori Kim. In order, it plays Sunrise first.
Then Blue Line.
Then Paper Boats, and then it says end of playlist.
Now the same Player class with Shuffled, given positions two, zero, one. Paper Boats plays first, because position two is the third song.
Then position zero, Sunrise, then position one, Blue Line, then end of playlist. One Player class, two behaviours, and not a single if statement about the mode.

scenes.title: Playlist: what to notice
bullets: One requirement became a type
One job per class
Repeat-one is a new class; nothing reopened
Announce the gaps: pause, volume, queue

steps.say: One requirement became a type: shuffle produced an interface and two classes. Classes come out of requirements.
One job per class.
Open to changes you didn't build: repeat one is a new class. That's Strategy plus the open-closed principle.
Announce the gaps yourself: pause, volume, queue.

scenes.title: Pause and think: where does 'repeat one' go?
bullets: Change Player
Change Playlist
Change none: add a new PlayOrder class

steps.say: Pause and think. The interviewer asks for a repeat one mode, where the same song plays forever. Which class do you change? Player, Playlist, or none of them?

scenes.title: The step-by-step answer framework

steps.say: Answer: change none. Add a RepeatOne class whose after returns the current position. Concept eight: the full framework, five steps expanded into eleven.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.4 The step-by-step answer framework

scenes.title: Eleven steps, applied to the parking lot

steps.say: Steps one and two: clarify and write requirements. Who uses it? One location or many? What must it do, and how well, for example thread-safe, extensible, in memory? Output: eight to twelve numbered lines plus out of scope.
Step three, use cases: for each actor, what can they do? Customer takes a ticket, parks, pays, exits.
Step four, entities: which nouns hold state or behaviour, and which are just values? Spot is a class, spot size is an enum.
Steps five and six, relationships and the class diagram: uses, has, owns, or is-a, and how many. A lot has one or more floors, a floor has many spots.
Step seven, key flows: step by step for the two or three main use cases, and which states the core object moves through. A ticket goes active, then closed.
Step eight, patterns and SOLID: is there a rule that varies? Pricing, so Strategy. Is there a class with two reasons to change?

Steps nine and ten, code, then edge cases and concurrency. Two cars grabbing the same spot? Exit before entry? Use exceptions and locks. An exception is Java's error signal that stops the normal flow, a lock lets one thread at a time into protected code.
Step eleven, extensions: what changes if requirement X is added? Short answers, maybe one extra class. Say each step out loud as you enter it. Your progress being visible is itself scored.
Spend eight to thirteen minutes on steps one to three, not coding at minute two.
Code two or three flows fully, rather than stubbing twelve classes.
Name one or two patterns with a signal, not six.
Pass time into methods and hold money as BigDecimal, Java's exact decimal, or cents. A double can't hold ten cents exactly, so sums drift.

scenes.title: From one line to a list of requirements

steps.say: Concept nine. Design a parking lot is four words. The design is about twelve classes. How do you get from one to the other without guessing?

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.5 From one line to a list of requirements

left.heading: Functional: behaviour
bullets: Customer takes a ticket at entry
Refuse entry when no spot fits

right.heading: Non-functional: quality
bullets: Two panels never share a spot
New vehicle type edits no class

steps.say: A requirement states one testable capability. Functional ones are behaviours: a customer takes a ticket at entry.
The system refuses entry when no spot fits.
Non-functional ones are qualities. Two panels never assign the same spot: thread safety.
A new vehicle type edits no existing class: extensibility. Without a list, the design has no edges.

head: Question
Parking lot answer
rows: Ticket, park, pay; admin adds floors

steps.say: Four questions, about five minutes. Who uses this? The actors: customer, attendant, admin, and the system.
What does each do? Each action is a use case: take ticket, park, pay. Most of the list comes from here.
What are the limits? Floors, spot kinds, rates. Limits become constants and checks.
What's out of scope? The only question that makes the problem smaller. If they say your choice, choose, say it, write it down.

scenes.title: The parking lot in ten lines, part one
bullets: 1-2: floors with spots; five spot types
3-4: five vehicle types; ticket at entry
5-6: pay at exit, portal or attendant; cash or card
7-8: tiered hourly rate; free-spot display
9-10: refuse when full; admin adds floors, rate

steps.say: Here's what good looks like. Floors with many spots, and five spot types.
Five vehicle types, and a ticket at the entrance panel.
Pay at an exit panel, a portal or an attendant, by cash or card.
An hourly rate that depends on stay length, and each floor showing free spots by type.
Refuse entry when nothing fits, and admins add floors, spots and update the rate.

scenes.title: Making each line checkable
bullets: Out: passes, plates, booking, refunds, multi-site
Put a number on it: max 10 seats, 10 min hold
Name the actor: a member can reserve
Saying no to extra scope is a strength

steps.say: Out of scope: season passes, plate recognition, booking ahead, refunds. If no line asked for it, it's not in the design.
Put a number on each line. Book some seats becomes: at most ten seats per show, released after ten minutes. A constant and a check.
Name the actor: a member can reserve, so you know which class owns the method.
Declining is strong: let me park reservations and get ticketing working end to end first.

head: Actor
Use cases
rows: Add floor, spot, panel; change rate

steps.say: A use case is one goal an actor achieves. A list is enough. Customer: ticket, park, pay, exit.
Attendant: collect cash, help.
Admin: add floors, spots, panels, change the rate.
System: assign spots, update boards, refuse when full. Every class you create traces back to one of these lines.

scenes.title: Finding the classes

steps.say: Concept ten: finding the classes. A ten-minute method. Collect candidates, cut the ones that aren't classes, and give each survivor one job.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.6 Finding the classes

scenes.title: Nouns become candidates, verbs become methods
bullets: Nouns: lot, floor, spot, panel, board
More: vehicles, people, ticket, payment, rate
Verbs: park, pay, leave, refuse, show free
A verb with no home = a missing class

steps.say: Step one: underline the nouns. Lot, floor, spot, compact spot, panel, display board.
Car, van, truck, customer, attendant, ticket, payment, cash, card, rate, hour. About twenty-two candidates.
Step two: underline the verbs. Park, pay, leave, refuse entry, show free spots. Each verb becomes a method.
A verb with no class to live on means a class is missing.

scenes.title: Five tests that cut the candidates

head: Test
Parking lot example
Result
rows: Spot sizes vs cash and card

steps.say: Step three: cut with five tests. Test one: is it a value rather than a thing? An hour is a number, a licence plate is a string, and cash or card are options of a payment type. Those become fields or enum constants.
Test two: is it just another name for a candidate already listed? Customer and driver are the same actor. Merge them and pick one name.
Test three: does it have state that changes? A spot is free, then occupied. An hour never changes. Changing state means a class.
Test four: does anything call it? Nobody asks an Hour object a question. Never called means it's a value.

Test five, the big one: different behaviour, or only different data? Compact and large spots differ only in which vehicle fits. That's data, so one ParkingSpot class with a type field. Cash checks the amount handed over, while card calls a provider and waits. That's behaviour, so two classes. Tests one to four cut twenty-two down to about fifteen, test five alone gets you to about twelve.

head: Class
One job
rows: Owns spots, finds an empty one
Collects money, says if it worked

steps.say: Step four, one sentence each. ParkingLot issues tickets and knows when it's full. ParkingFloor finds an empty spot.
ParkingSpot tracks its vehicle. Vehicle carries its plate and fitting spot types.
Ticket notes vehicle, spot and entry time. ParkingRate turns a duration into a price.
Payment collects money. The board shows free counts. ParkingLot's sentence has an and. Naming that tension out loud is enough.

scenes.title: Put the method where the data is
bullets: Find free spot lives on ParkingFloor
Price lives on Rate; ticket on Lot
Mistake: one subclass per value
Mistake: missing the ticket and the rate class
Mistake: the Manager god class

steps.say: Step five: put each method where its data lives. Find a free spot goes on ParkingFloor.
Pricing goes on ParkingRate, taking a ticket on ParkingLot. That's the Information Expert guideline.
Mistake: one subclass per value, like CompactSpot with no behaviour.
Mistake: missing the record keeper, a ticket, and the rule, a rate.
Mistake: a Manager god class owning everything.

scenes.title: Pause and think: car, van, truck
bullets: Three subclasses
An enum, if they differ only in which spots fit
Always a separate class per vehicle

steps.say: Pause and think. Car, van and truck: should they be three subclasses of Vehicle, or one enum called VehicleType?

scenes.title: Connecting the classes: a preview
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  L["ParkingLot"] -->|"owns 1..many"| F["ParkingFloor"]
  F -->|"owns many"| S["ParkingSpot"]
  T["Ticket"] -->|"points to"| S
  L -->|"uses"| R["Rate interface"]
  H["HourlyRate"] -.->|"implements"| R
scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.7 Connecting the classes (preview)

steps.say: Answer: an enum, if they differ only in which spots fit. Concept eleven, connecting classes. Five choices.

Dependency: briefly uses, like the lot calling the rate. Association: holds a reference, like a ticket and its spot. Aggregation: contains parts that live alone. Composition: owns parts that die with it, like floor and spots.
Inheritance: is a kind of. Then add multiplicity. The classic error is inheritance where composition is right. A car is not an engine, so Car has an Engine.

scenes.title: Keeping the design honest with SOLID

steps.say: Concept twelve. SOLID is five rules, one per letter. Run them as five quick checks on your own diagram, in about five minutes.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.8 Keeping the design honest with SOLID

scenes.title: Five SOLID checks on the parking lot

head: Check
Failure signal
Parking lot finding
rows: Lot: tickets AND spots, say it

steps.say: S, single responsibility: one reason to change. The signal it failed: the class sentence needs and. Our ParkingLot issues tickets and finds spots. Finding: split it if time allows, otherwise say it out loud.

O, open-closed: add behaviour without editing existing code. The signal: a switch or if chain over a type. Our pricing sits behind ParkingRate, so a weekend rate is a new class, not a switch edit. Passes.

L, Liskov substitution: a subclass must work anywhere its parent does. The signal: a subclass that throws or does nothing. A ReadOnlySpot whose occupy method throws would fail. Read every inheritance arrow at the end, since they get added late.
I, interface segregation: no class implements methods it doesn't use. The signal: empty method bodies. We have no wide interfaces. Passes.

D, dependency inversion: depend on an interface, not a concrete class. The signal: a business class constructs a technical one itself. If the lot did new CreditCardTransaction inside, you couldn't test it or add cash. It depends on a Payment interface instead. Passes. Two real findings is a good pass. Five means rework. Zero means you didn't look.

scenes.title: Where SOLID earns credit, and when not to
bullets: S and O earn the most credit
No single-implementer interfaces 'because SOLID'
Interface when a 2nd impl or test double exists
Don't over-split: one-sentence test is the line

steps.say: S and O earn most credit. What if trucks are charged differently? Add a class, not a switch branch.
Don't make an interface for everything. One implementer means pointless indirection.
Add one for a second implementation or a test double, a fake used in tests.
And don't over-split. The one-sentence test is the line.

scenes.title: The design patterns of this round

steps.say: Concept thirteen. There are twenty-three classic Gang of Four patterns. Six recur here. A misapplied pattern hurts more than an unknown one, so learn each with its signal.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.9 The design patterns that come up in this round

scenes.title: Six patterns, each with its signal

steps.say: Strategy. Signal: one operation with several interchangeable rules. Parking lot: ParkingRate with HourlyRate, WeekendRate and MonthlyPass. Without it, the pricing method grows a switch you edit for every rate. Skip it if there's only one rule.

Factory. Signal: what you create depends on a type value, and the caller shouldn't know the concrete class. A factory turns a vehicle type into a Vehicle, so the entrance panel doesn't know every vehicle class. A factory method is usually enough.

Observer. Signal: one thing changes and several others must know, without the source knowing them. The spot is the subject. Display boards and panels register and update when it fills. With only one listener, just call it directly.

State. Signal: behaviour depends on the current state, with a fixed set of transitions. A ticket goes active, paid, closed. Choose it only for big transition tables. For three or four states, an enum plus one guarded method is enough, and say why.

Singleton. Signal: exactly one instance must exist, like the ParkingLot. Expect two follow-ups every time: thread safety, and global state hurting tests. Many teams inject one shared instance instead.

Builder. Signal: many optional fields and a long constructor. A library BookItem with eight arguments is easy to mix up, since two adjacent strings compile fine. A builder sets fields by name. Mention it at about six arguments and move on.
Strategy: a Comparator passed to List dot sort.
Factory: List dot of, and Executors' thread pool methods.
Observer: Swing's ActionListener, Spring events.
State: an order moving placed, paid, shipped, delivered.
Singleton: Runtime dot getRuntime.
Builder: StringBuilder. Use one or two patterns, and compare: rate gets Strategy, ticket doesn't get State, because one guard is enough.

scenes.title: A machine-coding skeleton that scales
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  D["Driver Main"] --> S["Services: park, exit"]
  S --> ST["Strategies: pricing"]
  S --> R["Repositories: in-memory maps"]
  R --> M["Models: entities, records, enums"]
  S --> M
scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.10 Code, edge cases and concurrency

steps.say: Concept fourteen, interview code in five layers. Models: entities like ParkingSpot, records like Vehicle, enums like VehicleType.
Repositories store and find objects in an in-memory map. Strategies hold the rules that vary, like pricing.
Services are the use cases, park and exit. The driver Main runs a scripted demo.

scenes.title: Code habits interviewers notice
bullets: Pass time in: park(vehicle, nowMinute)
Money: BigDecimal or cents, never double
Fail loudly with clear exceptions
Optional when 'not found' is normal
private final fields, domain names

steps.say: Pass time in: park takes now minute as a parameter, so it's testable.
Money as BigDecimal or cents, never double.
Fail loudly with clear exceptions.
Return an Optional, a box that's full or empty, when not found is normal. Park returns empty when full.
Fields private and final, and domain names.

head: Category
Parking lot cases
rows: Lot full for this vehicle type
Exit before entry; round part hours
Two panels grab the same spot

steps.say: Input: null, negative, an unknown ticket ID at exit.
Capacity: the lot is full for this vehicle type.
State: exiting twice, exiting without entering.
Time: exit before entry, and do part hours round up?
Concurrency: two panels grab one spot. Use synchronized or a lock, or atomic structures. Lock the smallest thing that keeps the invariant: one spot, one vehicle.

scenes.title: Worked example: a small parking lot

steps.say: Concept fifteen. Now let's run every step of the framework end to end, on a deliberately small parking lot. Watch how each step feeds the next.

scenes.caption: Book: Ch 1 · 1.11 Worked mini-example: a small parking lot

head: Question
Assumed answer
rows: Out of scope: compute fee only

steps.say: Single lot or many? One lot, one or more floors.
Vehicles: motorbike, car, truck.
Spots: motorbike, compact, large. Smaller vehicles may use bigger spots.
Payment is out of scope: we compute the fee only.
Pricing: tiered hourly, round up, trucks double, swappable.
Concurrency: several panels at once.

scenes.title: Small lot: requirements
bullets: 1. Floors with motorbike, compact, large spots
2. Fit rules, smallest fitting spot first
3-4. Ticket on entry; refuse if nothing fits
5-6. Exit frees spot; $4, $3.50, $2.50 tiers
7-8. Swappable pricing; free count per floor

steps.say: Requirement one: floors with motorbike, compact and large spots.
Two: a motorbike fits motorbike or compact, a car compact or large, a truck large only. Smallest first.
Three and four: on entry, issue a ticket for a free fitting spot, or refuse.
Five and six: on exit, free the spot and return the fee. Four dollars first hour, three fifty for hours two and three, two fifty after. Round up. Trucks pay double.
Seven and eight: swappable pricing, and free counts per floor. Plus thread-safe, in memory, time passed in.

Use cases: the driver enters and gets a ticket, then exits and sees the fee. The admin adds floors and spots and changes the pricing rule. The system finds a free spot, refuses when full and computes the fee. Now the entities. SpotType is an enum of spot sizes.
VehicleType is an enum, and each value knows which spot types fit, smallest first.
Vehicle is a record: a plate and a type, pure data.
ParkingSpot is a class that tracks whether it's occupied and by which vehicle.
ParkingFloor holds the spots on one floor and finds a free fitting one.
Ticket is a record: which vehicle went into which spot, and when. It's the connection object, the record keeper beginners forget.
PricingStrategy is an interface that turns a stay into a fee, with two implementations: HourlyRate and FlatWeekendRate.
And ParkingLot issues and closes tickets. It's the service the panels call. Notice spot sizes are an enum, not three subclasses: different data means a field.

steps.say: The lot owns its floors, each floor owns its spots.
The lot keeps active tickets, each pointing at a vehicle and a spot.
The lot depends only on PricingStrategy, with two implementations.

scenes.title: Small lot: the park flow
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P["EntryPanel"] -->|"park vehicle, now"| L["ParkingLot"]
  L -->|"findFreeSpot type"| F["ParkingFloor"]
  F -->|"Optional spot"| L
  L -->|"occupy vehicle"| S["ParkingSpot"]
  L -->|"Ticket or empty"| P
scenes.caption: Find, then occupy, then issue the ticket

steps.say: The key flow, as a sequence. The entry panel calls park with the vehicle and the current minute. The lot asks each floor to find a free spot for that vehicle type.
The floor returns an Optional spot. If a spot is found, the lot occupies it and returns a ticket. If not, it returns empty, and the panel refuses entry.
On exit, the lot removes the ticket, releases the spot, then asks the pricing strategy for the fee using the vehicle type and minutes parked.
Strategy for pricing, not a switch.
Enums for types, not subclasses.
Ticket as a record, since it never changes.
BigDecimal, so three fifty plus three fifty is exactly seven.
Synchronized park and exit, so two panels never share a spot. Per-floor locks later.
No Singleton: inject the lot.
No State pattern: just active and closed.

scenes.title: Small lot: the Java, explained in words
bullets: VehicleType carries its fitting spots
Spot: null means free; occupy throws if taken
HourlyRate: round up hours, tiers, truck x2
park: find, occupy, issue ticket, or empty
exit: validate first, then change state

steps.say: VehicleType is an enum where each value carries its fitting list. Motorbike fits motorbike then compact. Car fits compact then large. Truck fits large only.
ParkingSpot has a vehicle field, where null means free. Occupy throws an illegal state exception if the spot's taken. Occupy and release are package-private, so only the lot can change a spot.

HourlyRate rounds minutes up to whole hours, adds minutes plus fifty-nine and divides by sixty, minimum one. Then it adds four dollars for hour one, three fifty for hours two and three, and two fifty after. For a truck, it doubles the total.
ParkingLot's park loops over floors, finds a spot, occupies it, creates ticket T one, T two and so on, stores it in the active map and returns it. If no floor has a spot, it returns empty.
Exit looks up the ticket, throws if it's unknown or if exit is before entry, and only then removes it, releases the spot and returns the fee. Validate first, then change state.
The demo: one floor with one motorbike, one compact and one large spot. A car parks at minute zero and gets ticket T one, spot F zero dash C one, the compact.
A truck parks at minute ten and gets T two, the only large spot.
A second car at minute twenty is refused. Compact and large are both taken. That's requirement four in action.
The free compact count prints zero.
T one exits at minute one fifty. A hundred and fifty minutes rounds up to three hours: four dollars plus three fifty plus three fifty, eleven dollars.
The truck exits at minute sixty, so fifty minutes rounds up to one hour, four dollars, doubled to eight.
Then we swap in the weekend strategy at run time. The second car now parks, and exits paying a flat ten dollars. Exiting T one again throws: unknown or already closed ticket.

scenes.title: Small lot: concurrency and edge cases
bullets: Lot-wide lock: find-then-occupy is atomic
freeSpots reads under the same lock
exit validates before it changes state
occupy throws if taken: second defence

steps.say: Why synchronized? Park and exit lock the whole lot, so find-then-occupy is atomic. Without the lock, two panels could both see the compact spot free and both take it. That's a check-then-act race condition, a bug whose result depends on which thread runs first.
FreeSpots reads under the same lock, so a display never sees a half-finished park.
Exit validates the ticket and the time before changing anything, so a rejected exit leaves the ticket open. Exit before entry, an unknown ticket and a double exit all throw.
And occupy also throws if the spot's taken: a second line of defence.

head: Follow-up
Answer
rows: New enum values; ChargingSpot if behaviour
Lock per floor, or a free-spot queue

steps.say: Electric spots? New enum values, and a ChargingSpot if charging has behaviour.
Nearest spot? A SpotSelectionStrategy, injected.
Update boards? Observer.
More panels? Lock per floor, or a thread-safe queue of free spots.
Cash or card? A Payment interface and a payment service. That's dependency inversion.

scenes.title: Study plans, by the time you really have

steps.say: Interview tomorrow? Two hours: the method, then the parking lot and vending machine.
One week? Chapters one to three, two case studies a day, then redo the parking lot from a blank page on day seven.
One month, about twenty hours? Add patterns and concurrency, one timed run in week three, and three more in week four.
Beginner? Six weeks, O-O-P first. Every plan ends with a timed run.

Fix

steps.say: Concept eighteen. Coding in minute two. Fix: requirements first.
No out-of-scope list. Fix: write it and decline extras.
One subclass per value. Fix: a field or enum.
A god class, or no record class. Fix: one sentence per class, and a Ticket or Loan.
Car extends Engine, or six patterns. Fix: composition, one or two patterns.
Switch on type everywhere. Fix: polymorphism or Strategy.
No lock, code that doesn't run, double for money. Fix: guard shared state, run by halfway, BigDecimal.
